content.text: Polymorphism is a core concept in object-oriented programming that allows methods or objects to take on multiple forms. In Java, polymorphism is primarily achieved through Method Overloading and Method Overriding.

content.text: Method overloading is a feature in Java where multiple methods with the same name can exist in a class, as long as their parameter lists differ (different number of parameters or parameter types).

items: Compile-time polymorphism because the method is determined at compile time based on the method signature.
It is possible to overload constructors too.

content.text: Method overriding is a technique where a method in a subclass has the same signature (name, return type, and parameters) as a method in the parent class. This allows the subclass to redefine the behavior of the inherited method.

items: Runtime polymorphism because the method to be executed is determined at runtime based on the object type, not the reference type.
Overridden methods in the subclass can be invoked even if the reference variable of the superclass is used.
The method in the subclass must have the same name, return type, and parameters as the method in the superclass.
The access level of the overriding method in the subclass should be equal to or more permissive than the method in the superclass (i.e., the overridden method cannot have lesser access privileges).
Private methods cannot be overridden because they are not inherited by the subclass.
The JVM determines which method to call at runtime based on the object’s type, not the reference type.
Method Overloading and Method Overriding are key concepts in Java that enable polymorphism.
Overloading allows the same method name to be used with different parameters, while Overriding allows a subclass to provide a specific implementation for a method already defined in the superclass.
Polymorphism helps in achieving flexibility and reusability in object-oriented programming.
